opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing was the freedom they gave me. When I arrived at MIT, I already had this fairly unusual idea that I wanted to build a programming language for computer graphics, which is not a typical PhD topic. A lot of advisors would have said, "That's too much engineering, go write some papers on a well-defined problem first." Fredo and Bill didn't do that. They trusted me to pursue something I was genuinely passionate about, even when it wasn't obvious how it would turn into a thesis. That trust meant a lot, and I think Taichi wouldn't exist without it.

The second thing is their taste. Fredo has an incredibly sharp sense of what makes a research contribution meaningful versus just incremental. When you show him a result, he immediately asks the questions that matter: Why is this interesting? Who will care? What's the simplest way to explain it? Bill is similar but from a slightly different angle. He has this deep curiosity and a very principled way of thinking about problems, coming from vision and signal processing. Between the two of them, I learned a lot about how to frame a problem and how to tell a story with research, not just how to get numbers to go up.

And third, honestly, they're just very kind people. A PhD can be stressful, and you go through periods where things don't work for months. They were always supportive and patient, and they cared about me as a person, not just as a source of papers. Looking back, I feel very lucky. A good advisor doesn't just teach you research; they shape how you think about your whole career, and I learned that from both of them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Fredo and Bill gave him freedom and trusted him to pursue his unconventional programming-language idea, rather than redirecting him to a conventional topic.

fable-5.1.text:
Working with Fredo and Bill was honestly one of the luckiest things that happened to me. The first thing I valued was the freedom. When I came to MIT, I already had this idea about building a new programming language for computer graphics, which later became Taichi. That's not a conventional graphics PhD project, right? It sits somewhere between compilers, systems, and graphics, and a lot of advisors would have said, "That's too risky, just do something more standard." But Fredo and Bill never pushed me in that direction. They said, "If you believe in it, go for it, and we'll support you." That kind of trust means a lot when you're a first- or second-year student and you're not sure yourself whether the thing will work.

The second thing was their taste. They have very good intuition about what problems actually matter. I tend to get excited about technical details, like how to make a compiler pass faster or how to lay out data structures in memory. Fredo, especially, would always pull me back and ask, "Okay, but who is this for? What does this enable that people couldn't do before?" That question shaped Taichi a lot. It's why we focused so much on making it easy to use, not just fast. And Bill has this way of asking very simple questions that turn out to be the deepest questions in the room. You go into a meeting thinking you understand your work, and you come out realizing there's a much more fundamental thing you haven't thought about.

And then the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that they're just kind people. They cared about me as a person, not only as a paper-producing machine. When I was stressed, when I was deciding whether to start a company around Taichi, they gave very honest advice without trying to steer me toward what was best for them. Fredo basically told me, "If you want to do this, do it, and the PhD will still be here." Not many advisors would say that.

So, if I summarize: freedom, taste, and kindness. I try to carry that into how I work with people on my own team now.

r001.rationale: Hu says his advisors gave him freedom to pursue his unconventional programming-language idea and never pushed him toward a safer project.

astra-6.text: What I valued most was the combination of freedom and guidance. Frédo and Bill gave me room to explore ideas that I was excited about, while helping me step back and ask what the important research question really was. It’s easy to get absorbed in making something work technically; the harder part is understanding why it matters and explaining that clearly. That balance—independence, thoughtful feedback, and encouragement—was really valuable to me.
